title_en: Supreme People's Court Issued Typical Cases of Judicial Protection of Intellectual Property
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Release of Typical Cases on Judicial Protection of Intellectual Property Rights

Case 1

Applicant Eli Lilly and Company, Lilly (China) Research and Development Co., Ltd. v. Respondent Huang Mengwei — Application for Act Preservation

(I) Basic Facts

The respondent joined Lilly China in May 2012, and the parties entered into a confidentiality agreement. In January 2013, the respondent downloaded 48 files owned by the applicants from the servers of Lilly China (the applicants claimed that 21 of these were their core confidential business documents) and privately stored the said files on a device owned by the respondent. Following negotiations, the respondent signed a letter of consent, acknowledging the download of 33 confidential documents belonging to the company, and undertook to allow personnel designated by the applicants to inspect and delete the said documents. Thereafter, the applicants repeatedly sent personnel to contact the respondent, but the respondent refused to fulfill the matters agreed in the letter of consent. The applicants sent a letter to the respondent on February 27, 2013, terminating the employment relationship between the parties. In July 2013, Eli Lilly and Company and Lilly China filed a lawsuit against Huang Mengwei with the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court on the ground of infringement of technical secrets, and simultaneously filed an application for act preservation, requesting the court to order the respondent Huang Mengwei not to disclose, use, or allow others to use the 21 trade secret documents allegedly stolen from the applicants. For this purpose, the applicants provided the court with evidentiary materials such as the names and contents of the 21 trade secret documents in question, a letter of commitment, and provided a bond for the aforesaid application.

(II) Judgment

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court reviewed and held that the evidence submitted by the applicants could preliminarily prove that the respondent had obtained and was in possession of the applicants' trade secret documents. Since the respondent had failed to fulfill the undertaking to allow inspection and deletion of the said documents, there existed a risk that the trade secrets claimed by the applicants might be disclosed, used, or leaked, which could cause irreparable harm to the applicants, meeting the conditions for act preservation. On July 31, 2013, the court issued a civil ruling prohibiting the respondent Huang Mengwei from disclosing, using, or allowing others to use the 21 documents that the applicants Eli Lilly and Company and Lilly (China) Research and Development Co., Ltd. claimed as trade secrets protected.

(III) Typical Significance

The amended Civil Procedure Law added provisions for the act preservation system, extending its scope of application to all civil cases. Act preservation measures are an effective means for rights holders to protect their rights in emergency situations. By actively and reasonably adopting intellectual property preservation measures upon the application of the parties, the people's courts can fully utilize the timeliness of the preservation system, enhance the timeliness, convenience, and effectiveness of judicial relief for intellectual property rights, and are of significant importance in strengthening the protection of intellectual property rights. This case is the first in China to apply act preservation measures in a trade secret infringement lawsuit pursuant to the amended Civil Procedure Law, highlighting the practical efforts of the people's courts to respond to social needs and strengthen judicial protection of intellectual property rights in accordance with the law.

Case 2

Foshan Haitian Flavoring and Food Co., Ltd. v. Foshan Gaoming Weiji Flavoring and Food Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Trademark Infringement and Unfair Competition

(I) Basic Facts

Haitian Company is the owner of the registered trademark "" (a device mark), which was registered on February 28, 1994, and the designated goods include soy sauce, etc. Weiji Company was established on February 24, 1998. Weiji Company used the characters "Weiji" as its trade name and prominently used the characters "Weiji" on its billboards and factory signs. After Weiji Company was exposed for illegally using industrial brine to produce soy sauce products, Haitian Company's market reputation and product sales were adversely affected. Haitian Company believed that Weiji Company's conduct infringed its trademark rights and constituted unfair competition, and filed a lawsuit with the Foshan Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province, requesting the court to order Weiji Company to cease infringement, make an apology, and compensate for economic losses and reasonable expenses totaling RMB 10 million.

(II) Judgment

The Foshan Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province held in the first instance that Weiji Company's prominent use of the characters "Weiji" on its billboards and factory signs infringed Haitian Company's exclusive right to use its registered trademark; the two shareholders of Weiji Company were engaged in the food industry and soy sauce production industry before the establishment of the company and should have known about Haitian Company and its products under the Haitian brand, yet still registered the characters "Weiji" from Haitian Company's registered trademark "" as their trade name, demonstrating malice to free ride on the goodwill of Haitian Company's trademark, causing public confusion or misidentification, and damaging Haitian Company's business reputation, which constituted unfair competition. Accordingly, the court ordered Weiji Company to immediately cease prominently using the characters "Weiji" on its billboards and factory signs, cease using the trade name containing the characters "Weiji" and complete the change of its trade name with the administrative department for industry and commerce within ten days after the judgment took effect, publish an apology to Haitian Company in a newspaper to eliminate the adverse effects, and compensate Haitian Company for economic losses and reasonable expenses totaling RMB 6.55 million. In calculating damages, the trial court inferred Haitian Company's losses due to damage to its business reputation based on the reasonable profit amount and the decline in profit margin that Haitian Company should have obtained within 16 days, and, taking into account factors such as the nature, duration, and consequences of Weiji Company's trademark infringement and unfair competition conduct, determined that the profit loss due to the decline in product sales was RMB 3.5 million; at the same time, the court included in the compensation scope the reasonable advertising expenses of RMB 3 million and legal fees of RMB 50,000 incurred by Haitian Company to eliminate the effects, restore its reputation, and prevent the expansion of the infringement consequences. Weiji Company filed an appeal but voluntarily applied to withdraw the appeal during the second instance.

(III) Typical Significance

This case is a lawsuit arising from the "soy sauce gate" incident in which Weiji Company illegally used industrial brine to produce soy sauce products, and it attracted high social attention. In its adjudication, the court effectively safeguarded the rights and interests of the rights holder by determining legitimate and valid civil liability. With respect to cessation of infringement, after finding that the defendant constituted unfair competition, the court ordered the defendant to cease using the relevant trade name and ordered it to change its business name within a specified period, completely eliminating the risk of further infringement. With respect to damages, in circumstances where there was evidence showing that the rights holder had suffered relatively large losses, but the existing evidence was insufficient to directly prove the exact amount of actual damages, the court determined the amount of damages by combining relevant evidence such as audit reports, so that the damages amount was closer to the rights holder's actual losses, providing maximum compensation for the losses suffered by the rights holder. At the same time, the court included in the compensation scope the reasonable advertising expenses incurred by the rights holder to eliminate the effects of the infringement and unfair competition, restore its reputation, and prevent the expansion of the infringement consequences, reflecting the strength and determination to strengthen judicial protection of intellectual property rights.

Case 3

Bayerische Motoren Werke Aktiengesellschaft (BMW AG) v. Guangzhou Century Baochi Garment Industry Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Trademark Infringement and Unfair Competition

(I) Basic Facts

BMW Company owns trademarks such as "BMW", "" (a device mark), and "宝马" registered on goods including automobiles in Class 12, and the trademark "" (a device mark) on clothing goods in Class 25. Century Baochi Company produced and sold clothing products bearing the marks "", "FENGBAOMAFENG and device", and "丰宝马丰 FENGBAOMAFENG and device", and prominently displayed the mark "FENGBAOMAFENG and device" on its website and in its stores, and used the business name "Germany Century BMW Group Co., Ltd." on clothing tags, websites, promotional brochures, etc. BMW Company filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court on the grounds of trademark infringement and unfair competition, requesting the court to order Century Baochi Company and others to cease infringement and to compensate for economic losses of RMB 2 million.

(II) Judgment

The Beijing High People's Court held in the second instance that Century Baochi Company's prominent use of the allegedly infringing marks similar to BMW Company's registered trademarks on its clothing products and in its promotional activities infringed BMW Company's exclusive right to use its trademarks; its use of the business name "Germany Century BMW Group Co., Ltd." on clothing tags and elsewhere violated the principle of good faith and generally accepted business ethics, intending to exploit BMW Company's goodwill for illegal profits, and constituted unfair competition. The evidence submitted by BMW Company was sufficient to prove that Century Baochi Company had obvious subjective malice in its infringement, with a long duration, wide scope, and huge profits far exceeding RMB 2 million, and the circumstances of the infringement were extremely serious. Additionally, BMW Company's registered trademarks involved in the case had high reputation, and BMW Company had incurred reasonable expenses to stop the infringement. To fully protect the legitimate rights and interests of the rights holder, increase the cost of infringement, and reduce the cost of rights enforcement, the court fully supported BMW Company's claim for damages. Accordingly, the court ordered the defendant to cease infringement, eliminate effects, and compensate for economic losses of RMB 2 million. At the same time, with respect to Century Baochi Company's malicious infringement, the court imposed a civil sanction of a fine of RMB 100,000, and issued a judicial recommendation to the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (SAIC), suggesting that it conduct a comprehensive investigation and handling of the infringement. In early 2013, the SAIC issued a special notice requiring local industry and commerce departments nationwide to investigate and handle conduct suspected of infringing BMW Company's relevant registered trademark rights. Local industry and commerce bureaus subsequently conducted comprehensive investigations and processing of free-riding and imitation activities involving infringement of BMW Company's trademark rights.

(III) Typical Significance

This case is a typical example of the people's courts increasing punishment for malicious infringement in accordance with the law. First, with respect to the determination of the amount of compensation, where the existing evidence showed that the infringer's profits from the infringement far exceeded the maximum statutory compensation of RMB 500,000 provided by the Trademark Law and the rights holder's claim, and taking into account factors such as the infringer's organized large-scale infringement, obvious subjective malice, long duration, wide scope, and huge profits, the court of second instance did not adopt the method of statutory compensation to determine the amount of damages, but instead used its discretion to determine the amount of damages based on the specific circumstances of the case, fully supporting the rights holder's claim. Second, in terms of increasing the cost of infringement, given the organized and large-scale malicious infringement by the infringer, and in the absence of prior administrative penalties by the administrative authorities, the court of second instance, in the spirit of increasing punishment, imposed civil sanctions on the infringer in accordance with the law. Finally, the trial court, having regard to other unhandled infringements discovered during the trial, issued a judicial recommendation to the relevant authorities, proposing corresponding handling plans. The industry and commerce departments actively acted on the judicial recommendation, effectively cracking down on malicious infringement and achieving good social results. This case demonstrates the determination and actions of Chinese courts to equally protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese and foreign intellectual property rights holders, maintain a fair and orderly market economic order, and strengthen the protection of intellectual property rights.

Case 4

Zhuhai Gree Electric Appliances Co., Ltd. v. Guangdong Midea Refrigeration Equipment Co., Ltd. et al. — Dispute over Infringement of Invention Patent

(I) Basic Facts

Midea Company produced four models of "Midea Split Air Conditioner" products, including model KFR-26GW/DY-V2(E2). Gree Company filed a lawsuit with the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province, alleging that the manufacture and sale of the aforesaid products by Midea Company infringed its invention patent titled "Method for Controlling Air Conditioner to Operate According to Self-Defined Curve," and requested the court to order the defendant to cease the infringing acts, compensate for losses, and pay reasonable expenses incurred in investigating and stopping the infringement.

(II) Judgment

The Guangdong High People's Court held in the second instance that the technical solution for the "Sleep Comfort Mode 3" operation mode of the KFR-26GW/DY-V2(E2) air conditioner infringed the invention patent in question. The installation manual attached to the accused infringing product clearly described the function of "Sleep Comfort Mode 3" and stated that the manual applied to the other three air conditioner models, from which it could be inferred that those three models also had "Sleep Comfort Mode 3." The four accused infringing products in this case belonged to the same series, differing only in power while having the same functions, which was consistent with industry practice. Midea Company argued that the functions of the three air conditioners were different and thus did not constitute patent infringement, but it did not provide corresponding evidence. In such circumstances, it could be inferred from the existing evidence that those three air conditioners also had the same "Sleep Comfort Mode 3," infringing the patent in question. With respect to the amount of compensation, Midea Company only provided data for model KFR-26GW/DY-V2(E2) air conditioner, from which it could be determined that the profit for that model was RMB 477,000. After the court of first instance explained the relevant legal consequences, Midea Company still refused to provide data on the production and sale of the other models. It could therefore be inferred that the profits for each of the remaining three models of air conditioners produced by Midea Company were no less than RMB 477,000. Accordingly, based on all the evidence in the case, the court ordered Midea Company to compensate Gree Company for economic losses of RMB 2 million.

(III) Typical Significance

Both parties in this case are well-known domestic home appliance companies. The case was complex and difficult, and had significant social impact. The court of second instance correctly applied the relevant laws and judicial interpretations, reasonably applied the rules of factual inference and the system of obstruction of evidence, correctly determined the facts of the case, and accurately determined the amount of damages, implementing the spirit of strengthening judicial protection. In determining the facts of infringement, after lawfully finding that a specific model of infringing product constituted infringement, the court reasonably inferred that the other three models also constituted infringement based on the descriptions in the manual relating to the patented technical features, combined with the specific circumstances where the party raised objections but provided no contrary evidence. In determining the amount of damages, the court actively applied the system of obstruction of evidence. The infringer held evidence of profits from the infringement of the other three models but refused to provide it. The court of second instance, based on the existing evidence, inferred that the profits for those three models were no less than those for the first model, and accordingly used its discretion to determine the compensation amount above the statutory maximum for patent infringement, increasing the cost of infringement for the infringer.

Case 5

Ashland Licensing and Intellectual Property LLC and Beijing Angel Special Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. v. Beijing Ruishibang Fine Chemical Technology Co., Ltd., Suzhou Ruipu Industrial Auxiliary Co., Ltd., Wei Xingguang, et al. — Dispute over Infringement of Invention Patent

(I) Basic Facts

Ashland Company is the owner of the invention patent titled "Method for Producing Water-in-Water Polymer Dispersion," and Angel Company is authorized by Ashland Company to legally use the said patent within Mainland China. The invention patent is a process patent for manufacturing a product, but the product manufactured by this method is not a new product. Wei Xingguang joined Angel Company in 1996 and served as General Manager of Angel Company and later as Business Director for Ashland China. He later left and became a shareholder and director of Ruishibang Company, and after the establishment of Ruipu Company, he also served as a director of that company. Ruipu Company and Ruishibang Company produced, manufactured, and sold a fully aqueous polymer concentrate identical to the product produced by the patented process in question. Although Ashland Company and Angel Company had collected evidence concerning the defendants' production process through various methods, including applying to the court for evidence preservation and notarization, they were still unable to obtain all evidence to prove the complete production process of the defendants. Ashland Company and Angel Company filed a lawsuit with the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province, alleging that the fully aqueous polymer concentrates produced and sold by Ruishibang Company and Ruipu Company constituted patent infringement, and that Wei Xingguang constituted contributory infringement, requesting the court to order the defendants to immediately cease infringement and jointly compensate for economic losses and reasonable expenses for stopping the infringement totaling RMB 20 million; concurrently, they filed a related trade secret infringement lawsuit against the defendants with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court.

(II) Judgment

The Suzhou Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province held that the product involved in the patented process was an industrial chemical preparation with a specific customer base. The rights holder could neither purchase it from the open market nor enter Ruipu Company's workshop to learn the complete production process. Ashland Company had exhausted its reasonable efforts and evidentiary capacity but still found it difficult to prove that the defendant had indeed used its patented process. Considering that Wei Xingguang and the key technical personnel of Ruipu Company were originally employees of Angel Company and had the opportunity to access the complete production process of the patented process, and that although Ruipu Company argued that the method and content of addition of certain substances in its production process differed from the patented technical solution, it refused to provide corresponding evidence to support its claim despite the court's explanation, it was highly likely that the defendant used the patented process to produce the fully aqueous polymer concentrate. In the absence of further contrary evidence from the defendant, based on the specific circumstances of the case, it could be determined that the accused technical solution infringed the patent in question, and Ruipu Company and Ruishibang Company constituted patent infringement. On this basis, the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court mediated the case, and ultimately the parties reached a mediation agreement: Ruishibang Company, Ruipu Company, and Wei Xingguang undertook not to use the patented process; Ruishibang Company and Wei Xingguang paid Ashland Company RMB 15 million as compensation for the alleged patent infringement in this case, and RMB 7 million as compensation for the alleged trade secret infringement in the related case.

(III) Typical Significance

This case is a typical example of reasonably applying evidentiary rules to determine infringement of a process patent for manufacturing a product through factual inference and reaching a high amount of compensation through mediation. Due to the difficulty in obtaining evidence of infringement, process patents for manufacturing products, especially those not for new products, have always been a challenge in intellectual property protection. In this case, the trial court, based on the specific circumstances of the case, where the rights holder had exhausted its reasonable efforts and evidentiary capacity, and where it was highly likely, based on known facts and ordinary production experience, that the same product was produced by the patented process, no longer required the patentee to provide further evidence but appropriately shifted the burden of proof to the accused infringer. At the same time, when the accused infringer could not provide contrary evidence, the court found that it had used the patented process. This method reasonably alleviated the burden of proof on the process patentee and was of significant importance in facilitating process patentees to enforce their rights in accordance with the law. Furthermore, with a view to properly resolving social conflicts, the trial court appointed technical experts as people's jurors during the trial to ensure the quality of fact-finding, and on the basis of clarifying the facts and the rights and wrongs, facilitated the parties to reach a mediation agreement with a total compensation of RMB 22 million, effectively safeguarding the rights and interests of the rights holder.

Case 6

Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Technology and Trade Co., Ltd. v. Johnson & Johnson (Shanghai) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. and Johnson & Johnson (China) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Vertical Monopoly Agreement

(I) Basic Facts
(Note: The provided text for Case 6 cuts off after "(I) Basic Facts". It appears the content for this case is incomplete or continues in the next part. The translation includes only what was provided in this part.)

Plaintiff Rui Bang Company, as a distributor of medical devices such as surgical sutures and staplers manufactured by Defendant Johnson & Johnson, had maintained a distribution relationship with Johnson & Johnson for 15 years. In January 2008, Johnson & Johnson and Rui Bang Company entered into a Distribution Contract and appendices, stipulating that Rui Bang Company shall not sell products at prices lower than those set by Johnson & Johnson. In March 2008, Rui Bang Company submitted the lowest bid in a tender held by Peking University People's Hospital for Johnson & Johnson surgical sutures and won the bid. In July 2008, Johnson & Johnson revoked Rui Bang Company's distribution rights at Fuwai Hospital and Plastic Surgery Hospital on the grounds that Rui Bang Company had unilaterally reduced prices. After August 15, 2008, Johnson & Johnson ceased accepting orders from Rui Bang Company for surgical suture products, and in September 2008 completely stopped supplying suture products and stapler products. In 2009, Johnson & Johnson did not renew the distribution contract with Rui Bang Company. The plaintiff filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, alleging that the clause in the distribution contract restricting minimum resale prices constituted a vertical monopoly agreement prohibited by the Anti-Monopoly Law, and requested the court to order the defendant to compensate for the economic losses of RMB 14,399,300 caused to the plaintiff by the defendant's "punishment" of the plaintiff for its low-price bidding in execution of the monopoly agreement.

(2) Judgment

The Shanghai High People's Court held at second instance that the relevant market in this case was the mainland China market for surgical suture products, where competition was insufficient and Johnson & Johnson had strong market power. The minimum resale price restriction agreement at issue had the effect of eliminating or restricting competition in the relevant market, and at the same time did not have any obvious or sufficient pro-competitive effects; therefore, it should be determined to constitute a monopoly agreement. Johnson & Johnson's actions of revoking Rui Bang Company's distribution qualification in certain hospitals and ceasing the supply of suture products constituted monopolistic conduct prohibited by the Anti-Monopoly Law. Johnson & Johnson should compensate Rui Bang Company for the loss of normal profits from suture products in 2008 caused by the above monopolistic conduct. Accordingly, the court ordered Johnson & Johnson to pay RMB 530,000 in economic damages to Rui Bang Company.

(3) Significance

This case is the first domestic case concerning a dispute over a vertical monopoly agreement, and also the first monopoly dispute case nationwide in which the plaintiff ultimately prevailed at final instance. It represents a milestone in the development of antitrust adjudication in China. The case involved a series of major issues regarding the antitrust analysis of minimum resale price restrictions. The judgment at second instance explored and attempted principles for legal evaluation of minimum resale price restrictions, allocation of the burden of proof, and factors for analysis and evaluation. The analytical methods and conclusions are of great significance for advancing antitrust adjudication and the implementation of the Anti-Monopoly Law in China. The judgment fully embodies and demonstrates the function of the people's courts in preventing monopolistic conduct according to law, and in protecting and promoting fair competition in the market.

Case 7

Jiangxi Yibo Electronic Technology Co., Ltd., Yu Zhihong, et al. — Criminal Case of Infringement of Trade Secrets

(1) Basic Facts

Defendants Yu Zhihong, Luo Shihe, Xiao Wenjuan, and Li Yinghong were originally employees of Zhuhai Saina Company. In their daily work, these four individuals had access to and mastered operational information of Zhuhai Saina Company, including customer data for the brand zone, South America zone, and Asia-Pacific zone, as well as sales volumes and amounts for 2010, and the cost prices, warning prices, and selling prices of Zhuhai Saina Company's products. They were obligated to maintain the confidentiality of Zhuhai Saina Company's trade secrets. In early 2011, Yu Zhihong and others established Jiangxi Yibo Company to produce consumable products such as toner cartridges for printers, and also established Zhongshan Wode Company, Hong Kong Aster Company, U.S. Aster Company, and Europe Aster Company to sell Jiangxi Yibo Company's products. Yu Zhihong, Luo Shihe, Xiao Wenjuan, and Li Yinghong took customer product purchase information, sales price systems, product costs, and other information of Zhuhai Saina Company that they had obtained through their work relationships, and brought it into Jiangxi Yibo Company and Zhongshan Wode Company. Using this information, they formulated the U.S. price system and European price system for some of these two companies' products, and sold the same model products to some customers originally belonging to Zhuhai Saina Company at prices lower than those of Zhuhai Saina Company. According to audits of the financial records and export customs declarations of Jiangxi Yibo Company and Zhongshan Wode Company, the two companies sold products of the same models as those of Zhuhai Saina Company to 11 of its original customers, with a total sales amount of USD 7,659,235.72. Based on the average gross profit margin of Zhuhai Saina Company's same-model products, the economic losses caused to Zhuhai Saina Company amounted to RMB 22,705,737.03 (RMB 11,319,749.58 for the period from May to December 2011; RMB 11,385,987.45 for the period from January to April 2012).

(2) Judgment

The Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province held at second instance that the actions of Jiangxi Yibo Company, Zhongshan Wode Company, Yu Zhihong, Luo Shihe, Xiao Wenjuan, and Li Yinghong constituted the crime of infringement of trade secrets. The court sentenced Jiangxi Yibo Company to a fine of RMB 21,400,000; sentenced Zhongshan Wode Company to a fine of RMB 14,200,000; sentenced Yu Zhihong to six years of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 1,000,000; sentenced Luo Shihe to three years of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 200,000; sentenced Li Yinghong to two years of fixed-term imprisonment, suspended for three years, and a fine of RMB 100,000; sentenced Xiao Wenjuan to two years of fixed-term imprisonment, suspended for three years, and a fine of RMB 100,000.

(3) Significance

This case is the largest criminal case nationwide concerning infringement of trade secrets involving operational information. The total fines imposed by the people's court amounted to RMB 37,000,000, setting a national record for the highest fine amount in a trade secret criminal case. This case is a successful example of the Guangdong court system's "three-in-one" model for adjudicating intellectual property criminal cases, highlighting the integrity and effectiveness of judicial protection of intellectual property rights, and fully reflecting the leading role of judicial protection of intellectual property rights. The judgment in this case, whether in terms of the calculation of the fine amount or the imposition of criminal liability on natural persons, demonstrates a direction of severe sanctions against intellectual property crimes.

Case 8

Zong Liangui and 27 Others — Criminal Case of Counterfeiting Registered Trademarks

(1) Basic Facts

In November 2007, defendants Zong Liangui and Huang Li'an jointly invested to establish a fats and oils company. From approximately August-September 2008 to September 4, 2011, they employed multiple workers to produce and sell edible oil bearing counterfeit "Jinlongyu" and "Luhua" registered trademarks, and also purchased and sold illegally produced "Jinlongyu" and "Luhua" registered trademark labels to others. Defendant Chen Jinxiao and others, knowing that the edible oil produced by Zong Liangui and Huang Li'an was counterfeit, accepted employment to engage in production and sales, with an illegal business volume of RMB 19,249,759.5. From the end of 2009 to 2011, defendant Liu Zhiyong and others, knowing that the "Jinlongyu" and "Luhua" edible oil produced by Zong Liangui's fats and oils company were goods bearing counterfeit registered trademarks, repeatedly purchased and sold them, with the amount involved reaching several million yuan.

(2) Judgment

The Henan High People's Court held at second instance that defendants Zong Liangui, Huang Li'an, and others established the company for the purpose of engaging in illegal and criminal activities, and their main activities were the commission of crimes; therefore, they should be punished as natural persons rather than as a unit. Defendant Zong Liangui was convicted of the crime of counterfeiting registered trademarks and the crime of selling illegally produced registered trademark labels. For these multiple crimes, he was sentenced to a combined fixed-term imprisonment of twelve years and six months and a fine of RMB 10,500,000. Defendant Huang Li'an was convicted of the crime of counterfeiting registered trademarks and the crime of selling illegally produced registered trademark labels. For these multiple crimes, he was sentenced to a combined fixed-term imprisonment of eleven years and six months and a fine of RMB 10,500,000. Defendant Chen Jinxiao was convicted of the crimes of counterfeiting registered trademarks and selling illegally produced registered trademark labels, and was sentenced to a combined fixed-term imprisonment of eight years and a fine of RMB 900,000. Defendant Liu Zhiyong was convicted of the crime of selling goods bearing counterfeit registered trademarks, and was sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of four years and three months and a fine of RMB 970,000. The other 24 defendants were also sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of varying lengths and fines of varying amounts.

(3) Significance

This case is a typical example of using criminal means to combat intellectual property crimes, maintain market order, and protect food safety. The high amount of criminal proceeds, the depth of harm, the breadth of impact, and the high amount of fines imposed are rare in the field of intellectual property adjudication nationwide. This case is a typical precedent of the Henan court system's "three-in-one" model for adjudicating intellectual property criminal cases, reflecting the spirit of the people's courts in strengthening criminal judicial protection of intellectual property rights and severely cracking down on intellectual property crimes. The adjudicating court comprehensively applied various criminal penalties, not only firmly convicting and sentencing the criminals, but also paying special attention to the use of property penalties to increase the punishment for intellectual property crimes, and focusing on economically depriving criminals of their ability and conditions to commit further crimes. All 28 defendants in this case were criminally prosecuted according to law. In addition to sentences of fixed-term imprisonment, fines were also imposed, with the total amount of fines reaching RMB 27,040,000. This effectively deterred intellectual property crimes, purified the market environment, and maintained the market economic order.
